title: Mara and the Winter
premise: Folklorist Jonah Iversen arrives in the snowbound village of Hollowmere to record its winter songs, dismissing the locals' refusal to sing any verse twice as superstition. When he transcribes and repeats a forbidden carol aloud, every mirror in his rented cottage begins reflecting the room one second late — and the lag grows, showing him things that haven't happened yet. The village's matriarch, Edith Marlow, reveals that generations ago the villagers bound a hungry presence called the Winter Guest to their songs: sung once, it listens; sung twice, it answers. As the lag spreads to the village's windows, water, and finally Jonah's own memories, he must gather the fractured villagers — including the mute girl Mara, who was 'invited in' as a child — and un-sing the carol at the exact moment of sunrise, sacrificing his recordings and, briefly, himself to the lag.
about_author: Coral Thornbury is the pen name of a former archivist of regional folk music who spent a decade collecting winter carols across northern England and Scotland. She now writes horror that treats songs, rituals, and inherited silences as doors left deliberately ajar.

chapters.title: The Road That Forgets Its Name
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. He arrives in Hollowmere by bus through deepening snow, recording field notes and mocking the village's lack of phone signal. The driver refuses to go past the church. Emotional beat: confident detachment, the skeptic's pleasant condescension, undercut by a first wrongness — no birds, and snow that falls without wind.

chapters.title: A Room with a Lagging View
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. He settles into his rented cottage, cataloguing mirrors left behind by the previous tenant, and interviews Edith Marlow about the village carols. She agrees to sing — once. Emotional beat: professional excitement shadowed by Edith's warning, 'Never ask me for it twice,' which he laughs off.

chapters.title: The Verse They Won't Repeat
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. At the village hall, an old man sings the Hollowmere carol for his recorder; when Jonah asks for a second take, the room goes silent and everyone leaves. Emotional beat: frustration curdling into unease as he replays the tape and hears a second voice beneath the first, singing the harmony a half-beat late.

chapters.title: One Second Behind
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Alone at night, he sings the recorded verse back to himself. The bathroom mirror reflects him raising his cup a heartbeat after he does. Emotional beat: the skeptic's first crack — he tests it scientifically, and the mirror passes every test except the one that matters.

chapters.title: Mara in the Glass
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV, shifting uneasily. He meets Mara, a mute girl who watches him through the shop window, and realizes the mirror now shows a small figure standing behind him in rooms where no one is. Emotional beat: dread braided with tenderness — the girl in the reflection seems frightened for him, not of him.

chapters.title: What Edith Buried Under the Snow
chapters.summary: Edith's POV. She remembers 1974, when the lag last came: her brother sang the carol twice and was 'invited in,' leaving only his boots. She recognizes the signs in Jonah. Emotional beat: guilt and grim resolve; she decides the folklorist must be corrected before the Guest finishes arriving.

chapters.title: The Village of Averted Eyes
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. He canvasses the village; doors close, salt lines appear across thresholds, and someone has chalked the carol's opening note on his gate — a warning or an invitation. Emotional beat: isolation deepening; the found-family thread begins as Mara silently slips him a page of her own drawings of the Guest.

chapters.title: The Second Voice on the Tape
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Analyzing his recordings, he discovers the harmony voice grows clearer each night and now sings verses no one taught it. The mirror-lag stretches to three seconds. Emotional beat: obsessive fascination — the collector in him wants to hear more even as he understands he shouldn't.

chapters.title: Invited In
chapters.summary: Mara's POV, rendered in her silent, image-driven perception. We learn she was 'invited in' at age six when her mother sang the carol as a lullaby twice; the Guest keeps a piece of her on its side of the glass, which is why she cannot speak — her voice is collateral. Emotional beat: aching loneliness and the hunger to belong somewhere whole.

chapters.title: The Lag Spreads
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. The delay escapes the mirrors: his kettle pours a second after he tips it; his reflection in the window waves when he doesn't. He runs to Edith's house and finally says the words he swore he never would: 'I believe you.' Emotional beat: capitulation and relief — belief as the beginning of belonging.

chapters.title: The Choir That Never Disbands
chapters.summary: Edith's POV. She shows Jonah the church records: every generation loses one singer to the Guest, who builds its choir from the invited. The carol isn't a summons — it's a census, and the Guest is counting. Emotional beat: weary institutional guilt; Edith has kept the village safe by letting it stay small and silent.

chapters.title: Snowfall in Reverse
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Time around the cottage begins running a second behind reality; he watches snow fall upward in the mirror-world and sees tomorrow's version of himself standing in the yard, waiting. Emotional beat: terror of predestination — the lag is not showing the past, it's rehearsing him.

chapters.title: Mara's Voice, On Loan
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Through the glass, the Guest offers her a bargain: her voice returned if she brings Jonah to the mirror at midnight. She nearly does — then sees, in the lag, the Guest wearing her mother's face. Emotional beat: temptation, betrayal, and the first act of loyalty that costs her something.

chapters.title: The Carol's Missing Verse
chapters.summary: Jonah and Edith's shared POV. In the church crypt they find the carol's suppressed final verse, cut from every hymnal: the instructions for un-singing — it must be sung once, in unison, by everyone the Guest has counted, at the moment the lag equals zero, which happens only at sunrise. Emotional beat: fragile hope built on a terrible logistical problem: the village must sing together, and the village no longer trusts itself.

chapters.title: Doors Opening in Empty Houses
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. The lag reaches five seconds; the Guest begins stepping through ahead of its reflection — footprints in the hall, breath on the glass, the recorded harmony audible in the chimney. Emotional beat: siege mentality; the cottage becomes a fortress of turned mirrors and Jonah stops being a visitor and becomes a neighbor worth protecting.

chapters.title: The Village Decides
chapters.summary: Edith's POV. She gathers the frightened villagers in the hall. Old grudges surface — who sang twice in '74, who let Mara's mother be blamed. Emotional beat: the found-family theme made literal: a village that has survived by silence must choose to make noise together, and the vote to sing is nearly lost until Mara walks in and writes one word on the slate: 'me.'

chapters.title: Rehearsal at Midnight
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. In the snowlit churchyard, the village rehearses the un-singing while the Guest's choir harmonizes from every dark window, one second late, learning their parts faster than they do. Emotional beat: communal courage fraying at the edges; Jonah realizes the Guest isn't fighting the rehearsal — it's attending.

chapters.title: The Hour Before Sunrise
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. The lag hits its maximum: the mirror-world arrives a full minute early, and Jonah watches his own death there — the Guest taking his voice as payment, as it took Edith's brother. Mara grips his hand and shows him her slate: 'it only gets what you sing alone.' Emotional beat: despair transmuted into strategy — the un-singing must be given, not performed.

chapters.title: The Un-Singing
chapters.summary: Full village POV, braided. At first light, Hollowmere sings the carol once, together, and the lag closes to zero — the moment the final verse requires. The Guest steps fully into the world to collect its choir and finds every voice joined to every other; there is no single singer to take. Mara opens her mouth and speaks her first word in eleven years, giving the Guest the one thing it never had: a voice freely given, which it cannot hold. Emotional beat: climax — terror, unity, and release.

chapters.title: One Second Early
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. In the aftermath, the Guest retreats not banished but balanced, bound now by the given voice: it must wait to be invited, and no one in Hollowmere will sing twice. The mirrors reflect on time, but now a heartbeat early — a warning instead of a wound. Emotional beat: exhausted tenderness; Jonah's recordings are gone, wiped to static, and he finds he doesn't mind.

chapters.title: The Folklorist Who Stayed
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. He burns his notes on the carol but stays in Hollowmere through spring, fixing Edith's roof, teaching Mara written music, becoming the village's first new resident in decades. Emotional beat: belonging earned rather than found — he was pulled into the middle of it, and chose to remain.

chapters.title: The Song They Sing Twice Now
chapters.summary: Mara's POV, her voice restored and narrating in her own cadence. On the first anniversary, the village sings a new carol — written by Mara, about the Guest, the lag, and the girl who gave her voice away and took it back. They sing it twice, deliberately, because some things should answer when called. Emotional beat: resolution and quiet defiance; the horror is honored, the family is whole, and the last line of the carol is Jonah's name.
